article.overview: An oxygen extraction demonstrator is an in-situ resource utilisation (ISRU) system that tests whether oxygen can be produced from materials available at the destination, such as the carbon-dioxide atmosphere of Mars or oxygen-bound minerals in lunar regolith, rather than being carried from Earth. The best-documented example is MOXIE (Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment), which flew inside NASA's Perseverance rover and produced oxygen from the Martian atmosphere in 2021 [1][2]. No lunar oxygen extraction demonstrator is verified as flown in this article. The lunar examples discussed below are concepts or ground-test activities.
article.description: An oxygen extraction demonstrator is built to show, at a scale much smaller than a production plant, that a specific chemical route can yield useful oxygen under real planetary conditions. A typical system takes in local gas or material, processes it, separates and measures the oxygen, and releases or stores the remainder. Because the purpose is demonstration rather than supply, results are usually reported as output rate, purity, run duration, energy use and the number of runs completed. These measurements show whether a larger plant could be built. The catalogue name describes a function rather than one design, so this article distinguishes flown hardware from ground-tested and proposed concepts.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose is to test whether oxygen can be made reliably from local resources and to measure how the process behaves under planetary conditions, including low pressure, large temperature swings, dust and repeated start-stop operation [3][4]. Oxygen has two main applications. The first is breathable air for crews. The second is oxidiser for rocket propellant: JPL estimated that a four-astronaut return trip from Mars would need roughly 25 metric tons of oxygen, and that a larger descendant of MOXIE, a one-ton converter, could supply it [2]. Demonstrator data also inform engineering choices for future ISRU plants, such as thermal management, dust filtration and power budgeting [3][4].
article.operating_principle:
The reference system described here is MOXIE. Martian air passes through a dust-trapping HEPA filter and is compressed by a scroll pump [3]. The gas is heated to 800 °C and passes over a nickel-based cathode in a solid oxide electrolysis (SOXE) stack. CO2 splits into oxygen ions and carbon monoxide. The oxygen ions cross a scandia-stabilised zirconia electrolyte and form O2 at the anode [3]. The oxygen is measured for quantity and purity before release. About 6 per cent of the carbon-monoxide-rich cathode exhaust is recirculated to the intake to prevent oxidation of the nickel cathode [3]. The stack has ten electrolysis cells in series, arranged as two five-cell stacks, and runs were performed in current-control mode [3].

A lunar demonstrator would need a different route, because lunar oxygen is mainly bound in oxide minerals in regolith rather than in a gas. A NASA hydrogen-reduction reactor concept called ROxygen has been identified in search results [5], but its full text was not read for this article, so its process details are not used here.
article.scientific_importance: A demonstrator matters because it turns an assumption into measured data. Before crews depend on local oxygen, planners need to know how much can be made, how pure it is, how much power and time it needs and how the equipment copes with repeated start-stop cycles. MOXIE's seven oxygen-producing runs in 2021 gave that kind of data for a Martian atmosphere [3]. The MOXIE team presented the work as preparation for human Mars exploration [3]. A lunar equivalent would have to address different problems, notably how regolith is handled and how oxygen is released from oxide minerals. For now, the Martian results are the most detailed published test of in-situ oxygen production identified in this article's sources.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power figure for an oxygen extraction demonstrator. The only example here with verified physical data is MOXIE, a specific instrument that operated on Mars. Its values should not be applied to other designs. No lunar demonstrator figures are given because none were verified in this run.

examples.name: Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment (MOXIE)
examples.type: Flown instrument on Mars, operated on the Perseverance rover in 2021; has not operated on the Moon

measured_2021_runs.derived_rate_note: Calculated by dividing each run's oxygen mass by its duration from the run table in [3]; not stated in the paper.

examples.purity: NASA caption states 98 per cent or better [1]. The paper lists a purity target above 99.6 per cent [3]. No single measured purity value in the reviewed text.
examples.scale_up_projection_kg_per_hour: 2 to 3 kg per hour, stated in [3] as a projection, not a MOXIE result
examples.qualification: Physical and power values are from the NASA instrument page [1]. Chassis dimensions match [3]. Mass has not been cross-checked against a second primary source.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The only verified dimensions are for MOXIE: a 23.9 cm by 23.9 cm by 30.9 cm chassis [1][3]. Dimensions for any other demonstrator would depend on its chemical route, stack size, thermal insulation and power system, and none is assumed here.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: MOXIE's mass is 17.1 kg (37.7 lb) on Earth [1]. NASA also gives its weight as 14.14 lb on Mars [1]. Mass determines launch and lander requirements. A demonstrator with a different architecture would need its own mass budget, and no other mass is asserted here.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: NASA lists MOXIE's rated power as 300 W [1]. A secondary summary reports only about 100 W available from the rover and about 10 per cent of that going to oxygen production, but this was not confirmed against a primary source and is not used as a specification. The paper does not give a separate power budget for the 800 °C stack in the text reviewed [3].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: On Mars, the atmosphere is about 95 per cent CO2 [3]. Surface pressure is about 5 to 10 mbar [3]. The 2021 run table lists ambient pressures of about 631 to 768 Pa, although the column definitions were not confirmed [3]. Air density can vary by a factor of two across the year, and temperature by about 100 degrees [4]. The instrument uses a HEPA filter to keep dust out of the intake [3]. It operates intermittently [1], and each run needed a warm-up of a few hours before about an hour of oxygen production [4]. The 800 °C stack must survive repeated heating and cooling [3][4]. Lunar requirements would differ and were not verified.
article.limitations: Scale: The 49.9 g produced in seven runs is demonstration scale. Larger plants are projections [3]. Power: NASA lists 300 W [1]. A secondary summary says only about 100 W is available from the rover, but this was not confirmed against a primary source and is not used in the specifications. Cycling: MIT reports that start-stop cycling creates thermal stress that could degrade the system over time [4]. Timing: Operation at dawn or dusk had not been demonstrated at the time of the MIT report [4]. Transferability: Martian results do not transfer directly to lunar regolith processing.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: MOXIE was carried inside the Perseverance rover, on its front right side [1]. It was therefore delivered as part of a rover, not as a standalone lander payload.
transportation_process: Integrate the demonstrator into a lander or rover on Earth, with thermal and mechanical interfaces checked before launch.
Launch it towards the Moon or Mars using a launch vehicle.
Transfer it to the destination body and deliver it to the surface by landing.
Deploy it and connect its power, data and thermal systems to the host spacecraft.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: MOXIE was fixed inside the rover rather than deployed separately [1]. A lunar surface demonstrator would need its own deployment method, which is not specified here.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: MOXIE operated on Mars from inside Perseverance in 2021 [1][2]. No lunar oxygen extraction demonstrator is verified as flown in the sources reviewed here.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lunar lander or spacecraft compatibility is asserted, because no lunar demonstrator was verified and no lander interface evidence was reviewed.

article.historical_significance: NASA's April 2021 announcement described the first MOXIE run as the first time oxygen had been extracted from the Red Planet [2]. The first run took place on 20 April 2021, sol 60 after the 18 February landing, and produced about 5.4 g of oxygen in about an hour [2][3]. NASA later stated that MOXIE completed all of its technical requirements [1]. The paper describes the work as preparation for human Mars exploration [3].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The evidence base is narrow. It rests on NASA instrument and news pages, one peer-reviewed paper and one MIT release [1][2][3][4]. The lunar concept source was identified in search results but not read in full [5]. Sources disagree on several points. MIT reports that every run reached the 6 g/h target [4], while the paper's run table gives roughly 5.5 to 5.9 g/h [3]. NASA's caption cites a peak of 12 g/h [1], which is not in the run table. Secondary summaries report 16 runs and 122 g in total, but those figures were not confirmed in a primary source and are not used. The mass and power figures come from NASA [1] and have not been cross-checked against a second primary source. No image assets were verified, so this article contains no images.

data_quality_notes: Run-level rates in the paper's run table are derived by dividing oxygen mass by run duration; the paper does not state them.

Sources conflict on the MOXIE production rate: MIT reports that each run reached 6 g/h, the paper's run table gives roughly 5.5 to 5.9 g/h, and a NASA caption cites a 12 g/h peak. All three are reported with attribution.
Secondary summaries reported 16 runs and 122 g in total; these were not confirmed in a primary source and are not used.
Secondary summaries gave MOXIE mass values from about 15 kg to 17.1 kg; NASA's 17.1 kg figure is used.
A secondary summary reported about 100 W available from the rover; not confirmed, not used as a specification.
ROxygen: search summaries disagreed on whether it has flown on OPTIMA; treated as unflown. The NTRS document 20110011479 could not be read as text, so its output and process figures are not used.
A Fraunhofer Mini-ROXY lunar demonstration document was identified but could not be read as text; it is not used.
The Springer link for the companion Space Science Reviews MOXIE paper returned HTTP 404; it is not used.
No image assets were verified from official pages in this run, so all image arrays are empty and image_urls_added is false.
